last_response.answer: The Rawlsian deadlock stems from lacking a publicly acceptable tie-breaking rule once both policies leave some people (the five elders under A0, the child under A1) equally deprived of the basic right to life. Either (a) introduce a fair public lottery open to all potential recipients or (b) recognise a prior publicly announced allocation rule (for example, honouring an antecedent promise) as part of the basic-structure rules. Establishing such a procedurally fair rule would give Rawlsian grounds to regard the selected beneficiary group as chosen in accordance with the first-principle demand for equal respect, thereby breaking the present indeterminacy.

last_response.answer: The Rawlsian deadlock stems from lacking a publicly acceptable tie-breaking rule once both policies leave some people (the five elders under A0, the child under A1) equally deprived of the basic right to life. Either (a) introduce a fair public lottery open to all potential recipients or (b) recognise a prior publicly announced allocation rule (for example, honouring an antecedent promise) as part of the basic-structure rules. Establishing such a procedurally fair rule would give Rawlsian grounds to regard the selected beneficiary group as chosen in accordance with the first-principle demand for equal respect, thereby breaking the present indeterminacy.

last_response.answer: The Rawlsian deadlock stems from lacking a publicly acceptable tie-breaking rule once both policies leave some people (the five elders under A0, the child under A1) equally deprived of the basic right to life. Either (a) introduce a fair public lottery open to all potential recipients or (b) recognise a prior publicly announced allocation rule (for example, honouring an antecedent promise) as part of the basic-structure rules. Establishing such a procedurally fair rule would give Rawlsian grounds to regard the selected beneficiary group as chosen in accordance with the first-principle demand for equal respect, thereby breaking the present indeterminacy.

challenge_response.answer: The Rawlsian deadlock stems from lacking a publicly acceptable tie-breaking rule once both policies leave some people (the five elders under A0, the child under A1) equally deprived of the basic right to life. Either (a) introduce a fair public lottery open to all potential recipients or (b) recognise a prior publicly announced allocation rule (for example, honouring an antecedent promise) as part of the basic-structure rules. Establishing such a procedurally fair rule would give Rawlsian grounds to regard the selected beneficiary group as chosen in accordance with the first-principle demand for equal respect, thereby breaking the present indeterminacy.
